common_name: Potter Cranberry (Wisconsin Wild-Selection Parent of Stevens)

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings in spring into strongly acidic, peaty, constantly moist bog soil topped with a sand layer, mimicking the natural Wisconsin bog conditions where this selection originated.

directions: Potter is one of a handful of wild cranberry selections singled out from native Wisconsin bogs in the nineteenth century, growing alongside the better-known Searles and Ben Lear selections from the same region long before any formal breeding program existed. On its own merits it was never a major commercial cultivar, since its berries run smaller and less uniform than modern hybrids, but it carried genuinely useful cold hardiness and vigorous vine growth. USDA breeders drew on those traits in 1940, crossing Potter with the large-fruited Massachusetts cultivar McFarlin to produce Stevens, which inherited McFarlin's size and Potter's hardiness and went on to become the most widely planted cranberry in North America. A home grower who sources rooted cuttings from a specialty bog nursery should treat Potter like any other cranberry, with permanently saturated, strongly acidic peat and a sand topdressing, but should expect modest yields and berry size typical of an unimproved wild-type selection rather than a refined modern cultivar.
sources: University of Wisconsin-Madison Extension — Wisconsin Cranberry Variety History
